title: An Okavango Horse Riding Safari Lets Your Riding Club Canter Through the Floods With Zebra
meta_title: Okavango Horse Riding Safari Planning for Riding Clubs
meta_description: Okavango horse riding safari for riding clubs: rider rules, weight limits, group sizes, best months and how to plan a Botswana trip together.
excerpt: An Okavango horse riding safari suits confident riders who want to canter among zebra and giraffe through Botswana's floods. Here is how a riding club plans one.
content:
An Okavango horse riding safari puts experienced riders on horseback among zebra, giraffe, buffalo and elephant in Botswana's Okavango Delta, riding five or six hours a day through floodplains and channels. Rides take up to eight people, camps have six to eight tents, and riders must be confident at all paces and weigh under about 90 to 95 kg.

If you organise a riding club or a group of friends who ride, this is a safari where your hobby is the whole point. This guide covers what Delta riding is like, who qualifies, how to fit a club into small camps, the best months and how our club and society safaris handle the planning around it, from Maun flights to a few days of vehicle safari at the end.

Quick Facts

  • Where: Private concessions in the Okavango Delta, northern Botswana, reached from Maun
  • Rider level: Confident at walk, trot, canter and gallop; no beginners
  • Weight limit: 90 kg at Kujwana Camp, 95 kg at Macatoo Camp (checked November 2026)
  • Group size per ride: Up to 8 riders; larger rides on request at Kujwana
  • Time in the saddle: Around 5 to 6 hours a day, up to 7 on fly-camp moves
  • Best months: June to September for high water and cool mornings
  • Minimum stay: 3 nights at Kujwana; 5 to 10 nights suggested (checked November 2026)

What Is an Okavango Horse Riding Safari Really Like?

An Okavango horse riding safari is a long morning ride through unfenced wilderness behind an experienced lead guide, followed by an afternoon of game drives, boating or rest. You ride among plains game rather than past it, across flooded grassland and through water up to the saddle flaps.

Zebra, wildebeest and giraffe tend to see a horse as another grazer and let you close. Elephant, buffalo and lion are different: guides keep their distance and occasionally ask the ride to move off fast, which is why the ability rules exist.

A typical day in the saddle

A riding day at the Delta camps usually starts with an early breakfast and a morning ride of around five hours, with a stop for a drink or snack in the shade. Lunch and a long rest follow through the heat. In the afternoon guests choose a game drive, a boat or mokoro trip (water levels allowing), a bird walk or a sundowner, and afternoon rides can be arranged at Kujwana Camp.

Between April and November, Kujwana also runs a fly camp: riders move out on a full-day picnic ride of about seven hours, sleep a night or two in en-suite tents, then ride back. It is the most expedition-like part of an Okavango horse riding safari.

How Good a Rider Do You Need to Be?

You need to be a fit, confident rider who can walk, trot, canter and gallop in open country, rise to the trot for ten-minute stretches and stay comfortable for five or six hours. Neither of the Delta's two established riding camps takes novices, and both can stop anyone from riding who turns out not to meet the standard.

The two best-known bases for an Okavango horse riding safari are Kujwana Camp, in a 90,000-hectare private concession on the Xudum river system in the south-west of the Delta, and Macatoo Camp, also in the Okavango Delta, with eight tents on raised platforms. Their rules differ slightly (checked November 2026 on each camp's published information):

RuleKujwana CampMacatoo Camp
Rider weight limit90 kg (200 lb)95 kg (210 lb); heavier advanced riders by special arrangement
Minimum age12 recommended; children must be strong, certified ridersOver 12
Riders per rideUp to 8; larger on requestUp to 8
Hours ridingAt least 5 a day; about 7 on fly-camp movesUp to 6 a day
HorsesHerd of over 60, 14 to 17 handsNearly 50, 14 to 18 hands
Tents68, including a two-tent family suite

Weight, helmets and insurance rules

Weight limits on an Okavango horse riding safari protect the horses and are applied firmly. Macatoo asks riders to bring a fitted helmet, and both camps expect insurance that specifically covers horse riding (often an add-on); Macatoo also requires medical evacuation cover and a signed indemnity.

Be honest about ability when you collect names for an Okavango horse riding safari. One rider who has only hacked out at a walk changes the pace for the whole string.

How Do You Fit a Riding Club Into Small Delta Camps?

A riding club fits an Okavango horse riding safari best by taking most of one camp and splitting into two rides by ability. With six to eight tents and eight riders per ride, a group of 10 to 16 people can fill a camp, so the guides, the pace and the evening fire are yours.

That is why a private Okavango horse riding safari beats booking single places. On a mixed departure you might ride with strangers of a very different standard. As a group you agree the riding level, the pace of the second ride and the celebrations yourselves.

Non-riding partners and mixed abilities

Both camps welcome non-riding partners, who follow their own programme of game drives, motorboat and mokoro trips, guided walks and seasonal fishing. At Kujwana they even travel to the fly camp and join the riders' picnic lunches.

If any of your riders are borderline on weight or ability, plan them into the non-riding programme of the Okavango horse riding safari from the start rather than on the first morning.

How group pricing and rooming work

Riding camps price per person per night on a fully inclusive basis, and rates rise in the high-water months. Because both camps are small, availability is usually the first problem for a club, so fix dates early, ideally a year ahead for June to September. We quote every Okavango horse riding safari group personally from current camp rates plus flights and transfers.

On our group trips the seventh place is free when six travellers pay, and members can pay separately. Rooming is usually twin-share; agree single supplements before collecting deposits. Our page on how to organise a group safari walks through deposits, payments and a sensible booking timeline.

When Is the Best Time for an Okavango Horse Riding Safari?

June to September is the best time for an Okavango horse riding safari: the flood is high, water riding is at its most dramatic and mornings are cool. May and October are shoulder months, January and February are hot, and the rains begin in November. The camps' month-by-month notes (checked November 2026):

MonthsWater and ridingTemperaturesBest for
January to FebruaryFlood unlikely; rain pools on the plains; cooler morning ridesDays 35 to 45°C, nights 10 to 20°CRiders who cope well with heat
March to AprilRain pools remain; game spread outDays 25 to 35°CQuieter dates, fewer crowds
MayFlood usually arrives; shallow-water canters beginDays 20 to 30°C, nights 5 to 10°CEarly flood, pleasant weather
June to AugustWater at its highest; deep channels to crossDays 20 to 25°C, nights 3 to 5°CClassic water riding, cold mornings
September to OctoberFlood recedes slowly; game gathers at waterDays 30 to 45°CBig game, hot afternoons
November to DecemberRains begin; brief showersDays 30 to 40°CGreen landscapes, fewer visitors

Pack for cold June to August dawns of around 3 to 5°C. For a broader look at the seasons across the country, read our guide to the best time to visit Botswana.

What Could a Riding Club Itinerary Look Like?

A good shape for an Okavango horse riding safari is five to seven nights at one riding camp, including a fly-camp night or two, then two or three nights of vehicle safari elsewhere in northern Botswana. Riders settle on their horses and non-riders get variety.

DaysWhereWhat happens
Day 1Maun to riding campArrive in Maun, short helicopter or light-aircraft transfer to camp, afternoon settling-in ride
Days 2 to 4Riding campLong morning rides, afternoon drives, boating or rest
Days 5 to 6Fly camp (April to November)Full-day picnic ride out, nights under canvas, ride back
Day 7Riding campFinal ride and farewell dinner for the club
Days 8 to 10Khwai, Moremi or ChobeVehicle game drives and boat cruises to see predators up close

For the final days, our 7 day Botswana celebration safari through Chobe, Moremi and Khwai is a good base to borrow from. Members with less time can add the 3-day Okavango Delta mokoro tour from Maun, which starts from USD 715 per adult. Flights, Luggage, Health and Safety for the Group

Most riders fly into Maun, usually through Johannesburg, and transfer to camp by helicopter (about 15 minutes to Kujwana) or light aircraft. Luggage on these small aircraft is limited to 15 kg per person in a soft bag at Kujwana (checked November 2026), so riding boots, chaps and helmet need careful packing.

Carry riding kit in your hand luggage so a lost suitcase does not end your Okavango horse riding safari before it starts; spare bags can stay in Maun. Bring worn-in boots, half-chaps, gloves and your own helmet.

Malaria and medical cover

The Okavango Delta lies in the malaria-risk northern half of Botswana. NHS Fit for Travel currently advises treating northern areas as high risk because of an outbreak, and lists antimalarial tablets, bite prevention and prompt medical attention for any fever after travel; read the current advice on the NHS Fit for Travel Botswana page and see a travel clinic before you go. Kujwana covers guests for emergency medical evacuation, but each rider still needs their own insurance that covers horse riding.

On any Okavango horse riding safari, listen to the briefing, ride in your given order and never leave the string for a photograph. For a wider view of the Delta itself, our Okavango Delta safari planning guide covers camps, the flood and budgets, and you can compare all our Botswana safari packages.

Insider Tips

  • Test riders at home: Ask everyone to ride several long days in a row a month before departure, including fast work outdoors
  • Weigh honestly: Collect weights in kilograms when people sign up, not after deposits are paid
  • Pick your saddle: Macatoo offers English or western saddles; say which each rider prefers
  • Pack for cold dawns: June to August mornings can be 3 to 5°C, so bring gloves and a warm layer
  • Bring your own helmet: A properly fitted hard hat is required or strongly advised, and insurers often insist on one

Frequently Asked Questions

Do you need to be an experienced rider for an Okavango horse riding safari?

Yes. An Okavango horse riding safari is not for beginners. The Delta's riding camps ask riders to be confident at walk, trot, canter and gallop, to rise to the trot for about ten minutes at a time and to stay in the saddle for five or six hours a day. Others join the non-riding programme.

What is the weight limit for horse riding in the Okavango Delta?

The weight limit for an Okavango horse riding safari is about 90 to 95 kg, depending on the camp (checked November 2026). Kujwana Camp sets 90 kg (200 lb) and Macatoo Camp sets 95 kg (210 lb), with heavier advanced riders considered only by special arrangement. Confirm each rider's weight with the camp before you pay a deposit.

How many riders can go out together on a Delta riding safari?

Both main riding camps in the Okavango Delta keep each ride to a maximum of eight people, and one camp says larger rides can be arranged on request. A riding club of 10 to 16 people usually works best as two rides split by ability, sharing meals and evenings in camp together.

When is the best month for an Okavango horse riding safari?

June to September is the most popular time for an Okavango horse riding safari. The annual flood usually arrives in May or June and stays near the camps until about October, giving canters through shallow water and cool mornings. October brings heat up to around 45°C, and the rains start in November.

Can non-riders come on an Okavango horse riding safari?

Yes. Partners, friends and children who do not ride can join an Okavango horse riding safari group and follow a separate programme with game drives, boat trips, mokoro outings, walks and fishing in season. At Kujwana Camp they travel to the fly camp with the riders and meet them for the picnic lunches.

Final Thoughts

An Okavango horse riding safari rewards a club that plans around the rules: confident riders under the weight limit, two rides split by ability, high-water dates booked early and a good programme for anyone who does not ride. Get those right and you have one of the rare safaris built entirely around your shared passion.
